title: Roblox
description:
Roblox was always at its best for me when I was playing it with friends. Back in the day, I used to hop in with my school friends and we would jump between all sorts of games depending on what we felt like doing.

Racing sims, idle tycoons, disaster games, parkour maps - there was always something random to play, and somehow that randomness was part of the fun. One moment we'd be racing around, and the next we'd be trying to survive some ridiculous disaster or failing a parkour section for the tenth time.

I didn't actually play Roblox for a very long time compared to some of the other games in my collection, but whenever I did play it, I was usually playing with friends. That's what I remember most about it. It was less about the individual games and more about having a place where everyone could jump in and waste a few hours together.

Looking back, Roblox was a pretty fun part of my school days. The experience itself could be wildly inconsistent depending on what you played, but with the right group of friends, even the most ridiculous game could become a good time.

title: Dying Light
description:
At first, I thought **Dying Light** was just another game sitting quietly in my library that I had claimed at some point and then completely forgotten about. It was one of those games I kept seeing in my collection and thinking, *"I should probably play this someday."* Apparently, someday needed a little assistance. Then one of my ex friends from my school days told me to give it a proper try. And that was it. I got hooked. There is something incredibly special about **Dying Light**. From the moment I started playing, it became very clear that this was not simply another zombie game. The story, characters, world design, parkour, combat, exploration, atmosphere, progression and presentation all come together in a way that makes the entire experience feel remarkably cohesive. The **story** is one of the biggest reasons the game left such an impression on me. It manages to be serious without becoming exhausting, emotional without constantly trying to force an emotional response, and exciting without turning every moment into a mindless action sequence. The characters are memorable, their relationships feel meaningful, and the situations they find themselves in make Harran feel like a place populated by actual people trying to survive rather than a giant map filled with targets waiting for the player. And then there is the **parkour**. Absolutely brilliant. Running across rooftops, climbing buildings, jumping gaps, grabbing ledges and desperately trying to reach the next safe surface before several infected decide that you look delicious is an experience that never really gets old. Movement is not just a convenient feature here. It is a fundamental part of survival. The city is designed around it, and once you get comfortable with the movement system, travelling around Harran becomes half exploration and half controlled panic. Then nighttime arrives. During the day, Harran can feel dangerous. At night, it feels like Harran has personally declared war on you. The change in atmosphere is fantastic. Darkness, limited visibility, different threats and the constant possibility of being chased transform familiar locations into something completely different. A route that felt perfectly safe a few minutes ago suddenly becomes a questionable life decision. The **combat** is equally satisfying. Weapons have weight, enemies react to being hit, and the game encourages you to make use of whatever you can find. There is a strangely enjoyable level of brutality to beating an infected with something that was probably designed for an entirely different purpose. The progression system also deserves a lot of credit. You begin the game feeling vulnerable and relatively powerless, but as you explore, fight and survive, you gradually become more capable. Skills, equipment and experience make the progression feel natural, and watching your character evolve from struggling survivor to someone who can confidently navigate Harran is extremely satisfying. What really surprised me, though, was just how much I enjoyed **exploring the world itself**.
View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Parijat (@parijatsoftwares)

Harran has a great sense of visual and environmental variety. Different districts, buildings, streets, rooftops, interiors and surrounding areas give the map plenty of personality. There is always something to discover, whether it is a useful item, a side objective, a hidden location or simply another place where the game can remind you that opening one innocent-looking door is sometimes a terrible idea. For a game released in **2015**, this is an absolute gem. The visuals, lighting, environmental design, animation and overall presentation hold up remarkably well. More importantly, the game has an atmosphere that cannot simply be explained by graphical fidelity. It knows how to use its environment to create tension, isolation, danger and occasionally even beauty. And despite being set during a zombie outbreak, the world does not feel completely lifeless. That is something I particularly appreciate. There is a constant feeling that people are still trying to maintain some form of normality in an abnormal world. Safe zones, survivors, factions and everyday activities give the setting a sense of life beyond simply "go here and kill zombies." It makes the darker parts of the story hit harder because there is something worth protecting. I also ended up introducing the game to some of my newer friends from my college days. I got them to play it, helped them through the experience and eventually spent time going through the series together. Watching someone experience the story, mechanics and absolutely ridiculous moments for the first time is a different kind of fun entirely. At some point, **Dying Light stopped being just a game I played and became a game attached to memories**. Late-night sessions, ridiculous situations, close calls, helping friends through areas, laughing at things that absolutely should not have been funny, and simply enjoying the world together all became part of the experience. That is probably why this game has stayed with me for so long. I genuinely struggle to find a meaningful negative point about the original **Dying Light** from my perspective. It feels incredibly well rounded. The story works, the characters work, the world works, the parkour works, the combat works, the exploration works, and the atmosphere ties everything together. Most importantly, it made me want to keep playing. And that, more than anything else, is what I look for in a game. **Dying Light is one of those rare games that I did not simply finish and move on from. It became a favourite.** A 2015 game that somehow sat unnoticed in my library for far too long before turning around and saying, *"Where have you been all this time?"* The entire experience is fantastic, the memories are even better, and getting other people to experience it alongside me only made it more special. **A genuinely phenomenal zombie game, an unforgettable adventure, and a masterpiece that still deserves to be played.** And yes, after everything I have experienced with it and the rest of the series, I have absolutely no hesitation in saying: **The Dying Light series is goated.**

title: Dying Light: The Following
description:
[Previous Review: Dying Light](?review=dying-light)

After finishing **Dying Light**, I went into **The Following** expecting more of the same. Instead, it took what already worked and moved it into a completely different setting, giving the experience a surprisingly fresh identity of its own.

The first thing that immediately stood out to me was the **story**. I really enjoyed what the DLC did with its narrative. The introduction of the mysterious, cult-like group and the strange beliefs surrounding them was a nice change from the more traditional outbreak-survival storyline. It brought a different kind of mystery into the world and gave the story a more unsettling atmosphere. It still felt like Dying Light, but it was not simply repeating the same formula from the original game.

And then there was the map.

**What a map.**

The Following takes us away from the dense urban environment of Harran and opens up a huge rural region filled with fields, farms, abandoned buildings, forests, roads and plenty of places to explore. The change in scenery alone makes the DLC feel like a proper new adventure rather than just an additional chapter.

Of course, a map that large raises one very important question:

*"Am I really supposed to run all the way over there?"*

Thankfully, the answer was the **buggy**.

The buggy completely changed how exploration felt. Driving around the countryside, upgrading the vehicle, running over infected and occasionally discovering that the road you were happily driving on has apparently been reserved for something much more dangerous was an absolute blast. The vehicle was not just transportation either. Its upgrades and customization gave it a sense of progression of its own, making it genuinely satisfying to improve.

The larger map also creates a different kind of freedom. The original game had you constantly navigating vertically through the city, while The Following gives you much more room to travel horizontally. Instead of jumping from rooftop to rooftop, you are racing across open terrain, searching for locations, completing objectives and seeing just how far you can get before something inevitably goes wrong.

And somehow, it still manages to make you feel unsafe.

That is one of the things I appreciate most about this DLC. Even with all the open space, the feeling of danger never disappears. There are still plenty of situations where exploration turns into survival, and the game does a great job of making the countryside feel beautiful and threatening at the same time.

Visually, **The Following is just as impressive**.

The natural environments were a fantastic change of pace. Fields, forests, dirt roads, mountains, farms and wide open skies give the game a much more natural atmosphere than the original's dense urban environments. It was genuinely refreshing to simply stop for a moment and look around.

There is something strangely beautiful about seeing a gorgeous landscape and knowing that there are probably several infected waiting somewhere nearby to ruin the view.

The environmental design also deserves a lot of credit. The shift from a heavily populated city to a rural setting changes the tone of exploration completely. Instead of towering buildings and narrow streets, you get sprawling open areas, isolated structures and long stretches of road. It makes the world feel larger and gives the DLC its own personality.

The **gameplay** benefits from this change as well. The parkour that defined the original is still there, but the buggy introduces another major way of navigating the world. Between driving, exploring, fighting, scavenging, upgrading and completing missions, there is plenty to keep you occupied without making the experience feel unnecessarily bloated.

I also liked how the DLC continued to build on the progression and survival elements of the original. You have more areas to explore, more things to discover, more equipment to work with and plenty of opportunities to get yourself into situations where you immediately question your decision-making skills.

Because, naturally, every suspicious location absolutely needs to be investigated.

Especially at night.

Especially when you have no idea what is waiting inside.

The story, the new setting, the cult-like mystery, the massive map, the buggy, the environmental variety, the atmosphere and the visual presentation all make **The Following** feel like a substantial expansion rather than something that was simply added onto the original game.

What I particularly appreciate is that it manages to be **different without abandoning what made Dying Light special in the first place**.

It feels familiar enough that you still know you are playing Dying Light, but different enough that the experience never feels like a simple repeat of the original campaign. The natural environments were especially refreshing after spending so much time navigating the city, and the massive open map gave me an entirely new way to experience the world.

And then there is the ending.

Without getting into spoilers, I really appreciated the direction the story took. It gave the DLC a more serious and mysterious tone and left an impression that extended beyond simply finishing another set of missions.

Overall, **Dying Light: The Following** was exactly the kind of expansion I wanted to see.

It did not just give me more content. It gave me a new setting, a different atmosphere, a huge world to explore, a fantastic vehicle, a new storyline and a completely different way to experience the Dying Light universe.

The original gave me rooftops.

**The Following gave me an entire countryside to tear through at irresponsible speeds.**

And honestly, I would not have it any other way.

**A fantastic expansion with a memorable story, a refreshing setting, beautiful environments and enough open-world chaos to make the buggy feel like both a vehicle and a weapon.**

It may be a DLC, but it absolutely feels like its own adventure.

title: Dying Light 2: Stay Human
description:
Before reading this review, I recommend checking out my reviews of the previous two entries first, as this one continues from that experience and some of my thoughts make more sense with that context. [Read my Dying Light review](?review=dying-light) [Read my Dying Light: The Following review](?review=dying-light-the-following) Now, onto **Dying Light 2: Stay Human**. After spending so much time with Kyle Crane and the world of the original Dying Light, I initially expected that we might eventually see him return in some form. Instead, Techland decided to give us a completely new beginning with a completely new protagonist. And honestly, I was surprised. But it worked. **Dying Light 2** immediately grabbed my attention with the way its world was built. It had a noticeably different artistic identity compared to the first game, while still retaining enough of that familiar Dying Light atmosphere to make it feel like part of the same universe. The architecture, the lighting, the vegetation, the ruined structures and the sheer verticality of the city all came together beautifully.
View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Parijat (@parijatsoftwares)

The thing that really got me, though, was the **post-apocalyptic greenery**. I absolutely loved it. There is something about seeing nature slowly reclaim a civilization that has been left to decay. Buildings are covered in vegetation, streets are overgrown, rooftops have turned into gardens and entire sections of the city feel like they have been surrendered to nature. It created a visual contrast that I found incredibly satisfying. The first Dying Light had its own atmosphere, but Dying Light 2 took the concept of a post-apocalyptic world and gave it a much more colourful and natural identity. It was still a broken world, but it was not just grey concrete and destruction everywhere. There was life growing through the ruins. And that completely filled the cup for me.
View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Parijat (@parijatsoftwares)

The **map design** is another area where the game really impressed me. The city feels enormous, and the verticality adds another whole dimension to exploration. Long, tall buildings tower over areas filled with vegetation, abandoned structures and remnants of the old world. Looking down from the top of one of these buildings and seeing the city stretching into the distance is genuinely satisfying. It is also one of those games where simply travelling from one objective to another can become an experience in itself. You are climbing, jumping, gliding, swinging, running across rooftops and constantly looking around for the next place to reach. And speaking of gliding... **The paraglider was a fantastic addition.** At first, I was not sure how I would feel about it because the original game had the buggy in The Following, and I absolutely loved driving that thing around. I genuinely missed having the buggy here. But the paraglider won me over surprisingly quickly. It gave exploration an entirely new feeling. Being able to launch yourself from a rooftop, glide across huge sections of the city and then land somewhere completely different made the vertical world much more enjoyable to navigate. Instead of simply climbing higher, you could actually use that height to travel. I went from missing the buggy to throwing myself off buildings with a paraglider and somehow calling that transportation.
View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Parijat (@parijatsoftwares)

The **story**, however, is where I have mixed feelings. I liked it. Quite a lot, actually. But it was **long**. Very long. There are a lot of characters, factions, revelations, conflicts and twists, and while I enjoyed watching everything unfold, there were definitely moments where I felt the game was stretching the journey further than it needed to. That said, one thing I genuinely appreciated was the timing of the major revelations. The sudden events, discoveries and exposure of certain truths were often placed at just the right moments. The game has a good sense of when to reveal something and when to keep the player waiting. There were quite a few moments where I was completely absorbed in what was happening because the game managed to pull the rug out at exactly the right time.
View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Parijat (@parijatsoftwares)

The **characters and world-building** also helped keep the long story engaging. There is a lot going on in this version of the world, and the different groups, settlements and personalities give the city a sense of identity beyond simply being a giant playground filled with infected. The environment often tells its own story too. Abandoned structures, ruined buildings, reclaimed spaces and areas that have been repurposed by survivors make it clear that people are not simply surviving here. They are trying to build something new from what remains. Visually, the game is stunning. The combination of huge buildings and overgrown vegetation might honestly be one of my favourite aspects of the entire game. The contrast between modern architecture and nature slowly reclaiming everything creates some genuinely beautiful scenery. There are moments where I would stop progressing just to look around. Which is slightly inconvenient when there are infected nearby, but apparently sightseeing during the apocalypse is important. The gameplay also retains many of the things that made the original so enjoyable. Parkour is still a major part of the experience, exploration remains rewarding, combat is still satisfying and the world is packed with activities and locations to discover. The improved mobility tools make traversing the city feel more fluid, and the expanded verticality gives you more freedom in how you approach different situations. That freedom is probably one of the biggest strengths of the game. You are constantly looking at a building and thinking, *"I wonder if I can get there."* And then you spend the next five minutes doing exactly that for absolutely no reason.
View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Parijat (@parijatsoftwares)

There are, however, a couple of things that I did not enjoy as much. The **Survivor Sense** did not feel as efficient to me as the equivalent system in the original Dying Light. I found myself missing the simplicity and usefulness of the previous game's implementation, and there were times when I wished the information was presented more clearly or immediately. The **grappling hook** was another addition that did not really click with me. It is useful, and I understand why it was included, but personally it never felt quite like my type of traversal tool. The original parkour system already had a rhythm that I really enjoyed, and while the grappling hook added more possibilities, I did not connect with it in the same way. These are relatively small complaints compared to everything else the game does well, but they were noticeable enough for me to mention. Despite that, **Dying Light 2: Stay Human** managed to give me a new experience instead of simply trying to recreate the first game. It gave me a new protagonist, a new city, a new visual identity, a massive map, a completely different approach to exploration, a paraglider, more vertical gameplay and a story that, despite being longer than necessary, kept me interested until the end. Most importantly, it made the world feel different. The original Dying Light made me love the rooftops and the chaos of Harran. The Following made me love the open countryside and the freedom of the buggy. **Dying Light 2 made me fall in love with a city being slowly swallowed by nature.** I still missed Kyle Crane. I still missed the buggy. And I still found myself wishing the Survivor Sense worked more like the original. But none of that stopped me from enjoying this game. There is something genuinely beautiful about Dying Light 2's world. The mixture of towering architecture, ruined civilization, dense greenery, open skies and post-apocalyptic survival created a visual style that felt fresh enough to stand on its own. ![Abandoned Poolside Image](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IntenseParijat/cdn/main/screenshots/Dying%20Light%202%20Stay%20Human%20Screenshot%202025.09.10%20-%2001.22.48.58.png) In the end, **Dying Light 2: Stay Human** was a very different kind of sequel, and I appreciated it for that. It did not bring back everything I loved from the previous games, but it brought enough new ideas of its own to make the experience feel worthwhile. The story had its rough edges and could certainly have been shorter, some mechanics did not quite suit me, but the world, atmosphere, visuals, exploration and overall sense of adventure carried the experience remarkably well. It is another game I will remember not just for what I played, but for **how the world made me feel while playing it**. A beautiful post-apocalyptic city, an unexpectedly enjoyable paraglider, an unnecessarily long story that somehow kept me invested, and enough greenery growing through ruined civilization to make me stop and stare at the scenery while probably being chased by something. **Dying Light 2: Stay Human is not the same Dying Light I started with, but it is a worthy new chapter that managed to carve out an identity of its own.**

title: Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines 2
description:
I went into this expecting quite a bit from it because the game had a lot of potential. And honestly, it is pretty good in several areas, but it also feels like there were quite a few things that could have been added or polished to make the overall experience much more satisfying.

I really liked the way the game handles its action, combat, and stealth. The different approaches to encounters can be fun, and using your vampire abilities never gets old. There are also moments where the writing has that strange mix of seriousness and complete absurdity that somehow fits the world surprisingly well.

![The only real question in life is whether the fucking you're getting is worth the fucking you're getting.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IntenseParijat/cdn/339e7f376a1097a6e0e7478dc11b48a63f18d08a/gamewall/vtm-bloodlines2%20(1).jpg)

Some of the dialogue was genuinely entertaining. Lines like this are exactly the kind of ridiculous but memorable stuff that made me enjoy the smaller moments in the game.

![Ego, anger, and dick measuring get us nowhere. But business, diplomacy, a level head? Now we're talking.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IntenseParijat/cdn/339e7f376a1097a6e0e7478dc11b48a63f18d08a/gamewall/vtm-bloodlines2%20(2).png)

The story kept me interested to an extent, although I wouldn't say it completely hooked me. One moment that did get to me, though, was saying goodbye to the detective. After spending so much time with the character, that farewell actually made me a little emotional. It was one of those moments where you suddenly realise how much time you've spent with someone in the game.

The biggest problem for me was everything surrounding those good parts. There is a lot of back and forth between locations, to the point where travelling around can start feeling more tedious than enjoyable. Some sections also feel like they needed a little more content, and there are moments where the game makes some genuinely goofy choices that can completely break the atmosphere.

The optimization doesn't help either. The game can feel surprisingly heavy despite what is actually happening on screen, and the inconsistent performance makes some parts more frustrating than they need to be.

Overall, Bloodlines 2 is a game with plenty of good ideas and some genuinely enjoyable gameplay, but it never quite comes together as well as it could have. I liked the combat, stealth, action, parts of the story, and some of its memorable dialogue, but the amount of backtracking, optimization issues, and unsatisfying elements ultimately bring it down to an average experience for me.

title: 007 First Light
description:
I went into **007 First Light** expecting a good Bond game, but I came out of it feeling genuinely refreshed. There is something surprisingly satisfying about playing a James Bond story that is not afraid to slow down, build its characters, and actually let events unfold instead of throwing one explosion at you every thirty seconds just to remind you that you are playing a spy game.

I liked pretty much everything about the experience - the story, the plot, the way events gradually unfold, the characterization, the technology, the atmosphere, and especially Bond himself. The game does a great job of presenting a younger Bond while still giving him that unmistakable personality. He feels confident, witty, occasionally reckless, and very much like someone who is still growing into the legendary agent we already know.

And then there was this moment.

![The most Bond-like way to ask for directions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IntenseParijat/cdn/6c2be3288afe791e6c67435cdff43f0afe8aef07/gamewall/007-first-light%20(1).png)

This entire direction sequence had me laughing. Bond walks up expecting information and somehow ends up getting the full **Khaby Lame experience**. No explanation. No unnecessary dialogue. Just hands, pointing, and absolute confidence that somehow I am supposed to understand the geography of the place.

Honestly, 10/10 directions. Google Maps could never.

What impressed me most, though, was how much personality the game has. The story does not feel like it is simply trying to recreate the most famous Bond moments. Instead, it feels like it is building its own identity around Bond, his relationships, his decisions, and the situations he gets himself into. There is a nice balance between serious espionage, character moments, action, and the occasional bit of humor that keeps the whole thing from becoming overly dramatic.

The technology and presentation are also a major part of the experience. The environments look fantastic, the animations help sell the characters, and the overall presentation gives the game that modern Bond feeling without completely losing the charm of the franchise. There is a sense that the developers actually cared about making the world feel stylish rather than simply making everything shiny for the sake of being shiny.

And then there is Bond himself.

The characterization is probably one of the strongest parts of the game for me. He is not just "James Bond because the game says so." His personality comes through in the way he speaks, reacts, investigates, and deals with other people. There is enough confidence and arrogance to make him recognizable, but also enough vulnerability and uncertainty to make him feel like an actual character rather than a walking collection of one-liners.

![James Bond will return](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IntenseParijat/cdn/6c2be3288afe791e6c67435cdff43f0afe8aef07/gamewall/007-first-light%20(2).png)

Seeing **"James Bond Will Return"** after everything that happened gave me that rare feeling of actually being glad I played through a game. It is easy for games to become something you finish simply because you started them. **First Light** did not feel like that to me. It actually felt like an experience I was happy to spend my time with.

That said, the one area where I definitely felt some frustration was **optimization**.

After playing for several hours, the game can start to develop noticeable stuttering, to the point where I would eventually have to close the game completely and restart it. It was not simply a matter of running settings too high either. Some explosion-heavy and particularly demanding combat sequences would still stutter even after dropping the settings to low. So while the overall presentation is impressive, there are clearly moments where the performance struggles to keep up with what is happening on screen.

It is a shame because when the game is running properly, it looks and feels fantastic. Nothing breaks immersion quite like being in the middle of an intense Bond action sequence, explosions going off everywhere, the music kicking in, and suddenly the game decides it would like to experience those explosions one frame at a time.

![007 First Light credits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IntenseParijat/cdn/6c2be3288afe791e6c67435cdff43f0afe8aef07/gamewall/007-first-light%20(3).png)

But despite those performance issues, **007 First Light genuinely surprised me**. The story, the pacing, the characters, Bond's personality, the visual presentation, and the overall atmosphere all came together in a way that felt surprisingly fresh.

I came away from this game feeling like I had just watched a Bond film that I was allowed to personally interfere with, occasionally make questionable decisions in, and apparently ask random people for directions with the help of interpretive hand gestures.

The stuttering needs work, without a doubt. But everything else?

**This truly refreshed me.**

For me, **007 First Light** was not just another game with a famous name attached to it. It felt like a genuine attempt to give Bond a new adventure and let the character breathe. And honestly, that was more than enough to make the experience memorable.

**007 First Light - shaken, stirred, occasionally stuttering, but ultimately a damn good time.**
